mcqs.question: What's the correct rule for deciding what belongs at a CDN?
options: Any GET request is automatically safe to cache at the CDN
CDNs should only be used for JavaScript and CSS files, never HTML or images
CDN for static, shared, cacheable GET requests; origin for personalized, write, or auth-gated requests
Write requests should always be cached at the CDN to reduce load on the origin
mcqs.explanation: The rule hinges on whether a response is the same for every caller and doesn't have side effects — static, shared GETs qualify, personalized or auth-gated responses and any writes don't. GET-ness alone isn't sufficient (a personalized GET still fails the rule), CDNs handle HTML and images just as well as JS/CSS, and caching a write would prevent it from ever reaching the origin to take effect.

mcqs.question: A blog page has a mostly-static body and a live comment count that changes constantly. What's the right CDN approach?
options: Cache the entire page, including the comment count, at the CDN with a 1-hour TTL
Cache the static body and images at the CDN with a longer TTL, and fetch the live comment count separately, bypassing the CDN cache
Never cache any part of the page, since the comment count changes
Cache only the comment count at the CDN and serve the body live from the origin
mcqs.explanation: Fragmenting the page lets the slow-changing majority benefit from CDN caching while the fast-changing comment count stays live — the same principle as splitting cacheable and non-cacheable fields anywhere else. Caching the whole page makes the comment count wrong for up to an hour; caching nothing wastes the win available on the static parts; and caching only the volatile piece inverts the logic entirely.

mcqs.question: How can you put a mostly-static page behind a CDN when it contains one personalized widget?
options: It's not possible to CDN a page that contains any personalized content
Cache the whole page for exactly one second to limit exposure of the personalized part
Duplicate the entire cached page once per user so each cached version is safe
Cache the static shell at the CDN normally, and use edge includes or fragment caching to fetch and stitch in the personalized widget fresh on every request
mcqs.explanation: Edge includes let the CDN cache the shared shell while fetching the personalized fragment live and assembling the final response at the edge — the personalized part is simply never cached. A short TTL doesn't make a personalized response safe to share across users at all, and per-user duplication at the CDN is the pattern this technique specifically avoids because it doesn't scale.

mcqs.question: A team assumes an authenticated per-user API response is safe to cache at the CDN "because it's a GET." What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: Being a GET only means the request should be side-effect-free — it says nothing about whether the response is identical for every caller, which is the actual requirement for CDN caching
GET requests can never be cached under any circumstances
Authenticated responses are always safe to cache as long as the connection uses HTTPS
The issue only occurs when the CDN provider doesn't support cookies
mcqs.explanation: GET-ness is about the request having no side effects, not about the response being shareable — a personalized GET response still varies per caller and shouldn't be cached as if it were shared. GETs are cached constantly in practice, HTTPS protects data in transit but says nothing about cache scoping, and the risk has nothing to do with cookie support specifically.
